content: 1. Baggaley et al. conducted a literature review in 2015 to assess attitudes and acceptability of HIV self-testing among key populations. Their findings were published in AIDS and Behavior. 2. Brouard et al. investigated the prevalence of Hepatitis C Virus (HCV) and Hepatitis B Virus (HBV) in the general population in 2016 using home blood self-sampling and screening history. This study contributed to the development of a new French screening strategy and was published in BMC Infectious Diseases in 2019. 3. O'Brien et al. evaluated the detection of Hepatitis C antibodies using at-home collection kits and an innovative laboratory algorithm. Their findings were published in Infectious Diseases in Clinical Practice in 2001. 4. Jamil et al. studied the prevalence of Hepatitis C virus antibodies among Arab and Chaldean Americans in Southeast Michigan, USA. Their research was published in Ethnicity and Disease in 2013. 5. Kimble et al. conducted a clinical evaluation of a rapid immunoassay for Hepatitis C antibodies using self-collected oral fluid specimens. The results were published in Diagnostic Microbiology & Infectious Disease in 2019. 6. Quoilin et al. performed a population-based prevalence study of Hepatitis A, B, and C viruses using oral fluid samples in Flanders, Belgium. Their findings were published in European Journal of Epidemiology in 2007. 7. Barocas et al. assessed the acceptability of rapid point-of-care Hepatitis C tests among people who inject drugs and utilize syringe-exchange programs. Their study was published in Open Forum Infectious Diseases in 2016. 8. Bradshaw et al. explored the screening of injecting drug users for sexually transmitted infections and bloodborne viruses using street outreach and self-collected sampling. Their findings were published in Sexually Transmitted Infections in 2005. 9. Broad et al. implemented peer outreach point-of-care testing as a bridge to Hepatitis C care for people who inject drugs in Toronto, Canada. Their study was published in International Journal of Drug Policy in 2020. 10. Lazarus et al. described the Copenhagen Test and Treat Hepatitis C intervention study, which utilized a mobile clinic to enhance the HCV care cascade for people who inject drugs. This protocol was published in BMJ Open in 2020. 11. Morano et al. outlined strategies for Hepatitis C testing and linkage to care for vulnerable populations, including point-of-care and standard HCV testing in a mobile medical clinic. Their findings were published in Journal of Community Health in 2014. 12. Noller and Bourke evaluated the use of point-of-care rapid testing for Hepatitis C antibodies at needle exchanges in New Zealand. Their study was published in the New Zealand Medical Journal in 2020. 13. Persico et al. implemented an HCV point-of-care screening program and treatment options for people who use drugs in a metropolitan area of Southern Italy. Their findings were published in Liver International in 2019. 14. Solomon et al. demonstrated that integrating HCV testing with HIV programs improved Hepatitis C outcomes in people who inject drugs. This cluster-randomized trial was published in the Journal of Hepatology in 2019. 15. Williams et al. conducted a feasibility study on point-of-care Hepatitis C testing from needle and syringe programs in Australia. Their findings were published in the International Journal of Drug Policy in 2019. 16. Wong et al. targeted Hepatitis C screening among ex-injection drug users in the community. Their study was published in Journal of Gastroenterology and Hepatology in 2014. 17. Avramovic et al. described the HepCare Europe service innovation project, which characterized the patient population with active HCV infection as defined by HCV RNA. Their findings were published in the International Journal of Infectious Diseases in 2020. 18. Reipold et al. assessed the usability and acceptability of self-testing for Hepatitis C virus infection among the general population in the Nile Delta region of Egypt. This study was published on Research Square in 2021. 19. Walker et al. analyzed the costs of using antibody self-tests to diagnose Hepatitis C virus infection in four lowand middle-income country settings. Their findings were presented at the IHEA Congress in 2021. 20. Guyatt et al. provided guidelines for rating the quality of evidence, focusing on indirectness, as part of the GRADE framework. This was published in the Journal of Clinical Epidemiology in 2011. 21. A comprehensive search strategy was employed to identify relevant studies on Hepatitis C testing, including terms such as Hepatitis C, HCV, self-testing, home sampling, and point-of-care systems. Databases searched included PubMed, Scopus, PsycINFO, and CINAHL, with no filters or limits applied. The search was conducted on December 16, 2020, yielding thousands of records. 22. Conference abstracts from major meetings, including the International AIDS Society, EASL, AASLD, and others, were reviewed for relevant studies on Hepatitis C and HIV co-infection and testing strategies. 23. A detailed summary of included studies highlighted various HIV self-testing distribution methods, delivery settings, and support models. These studies spanned multiple countries and populations, including general populations, men who have sex with men (MSM), transgender women (TGW), and people who inject drugs (PWID).
